hook.support: How do you learn a new thing? Lots of people watch a video. Now you make one. Teach a work skill in under three minutes.
hook.core: Stuck on how to change a bike tyre, tie a tie or set up a router? You probably watched a video. Now flip it: you’re the expert. Pick a task from a workplace you know, and teach it in under three minutes, clearly enough that a new starter could do it after one watch.
hook.extend: Workplaces now train staff and help customers with how-to videos. Making a good one takes three skills: writing clear steps, speaking clearly, and putting shots in order. All of it is shaped for a viewer who has never done the task.

why.support: Videos help people learn. Making one shows you really know the job.
why.core: Workplaces use short videos to train new staff. Making one uses writing, speaking and planning skills employers value.
why.extend: Making how-to content for a real workplace is a skill you can use in training, trades, shops, cafés and online content.

articles.title: Teach it on screen

body.support:
An **explainer video** shows how to do something. Lots of workplaces use them to train new staff.

**Who is it for?** A new worker. They have never done the task. Every step must be clear.

**Plan it.**
- Pick **one** task. Keep it short. Under three minutes.
- Write the steps in order.
- Make a **storyboard**. Draw a box for each **shot**. Show what the camera sees.
- Write a **script**. Say what you are doing in each shot.
.
**Film it.**
- Use **close-ups** of hands doing the task.
- Hold the camera still.
- Film in good light.
- Speak clearly.
- Put safety warnings before the risky step.
.
**Test it.** Show it to someone new. Can they do the task after watching? If not, fix it.
body.core:
An **explainer video** teaches one task, step by step. Workplaces use them for training, safety and customer help.

**Purpose and audience.** The purpose is to **instruct**. The audience is someone who has never done the task. They might be watching on a phone, on a break, with the sound off. That shapes everything.

**1. Choose one task.** Pick something from a workplace you know: closing a till, folding a T-shirt display, cleaning a coffee machine, checking tyre pressure. Keep it under three minutes.

**2. Write the steps.** Use procedure skills: action words first, one action per step, exact details, warnings before risky steps.

**3. Storyboard.** A **storyboard** is a row of boxes, one per **shot**. In each box, sketch what the camera sees and note what you’ll say.

**4. Script.** Write the narration.
- Open with what you’ll teach and why it matters (5 seconds).
- Signpost each step: “First…”, “Next…”, “Finally…”.
- Say what the viewer sees, as they see it.
- End with a quick recap and a finish check.
.
**5. Film.**
- **Close-ups** for detail. Wide shots to show where things are.
- Steady camera, good light, quiet room.
- Speak slowly and clearly, on camera or as a **voice-over**.
- Add **captions** for key steps and warnings.
.
**6. Test.** Show it to someone who has never done the task. Watch them try it. Fix any step where they get stuck.
body.extend:
Instructional video is now a mainstream training format, used for staff induction, safety, product support and skills. Its purpose is to **instruct**. Its audience is a novice, often watching on a small screen, possibly without sound, possibly while trying the task.

**Planning.** Choose a single, well-bounded task from a real workplace, achievable in under three minutes. Break it into a **sequence** of steps using procedural conventions: imperative verbs, one action per step, precise detail, and warnings placed before hazards.

**Storyboarding.** A **storyboard** maps each **shot** to its content: framing (wide to orient, **close-up** for detail), what happens, and the narration or **caption** that goes with it. It is the visual equivalent of a procedure.

**Scripting.** Narration should:
- open with the purpose and the outcome.
- signpost each step and its relationship to the next.
- describe what is on screen as it appears; word and image must match.
- close with a recap and a finish check.

**Production.** Steady framing, adequate light, clear audio. Deliver narration with controlled pace, pauses between steps, and clear intonation, on camera or as **voice-over**. Use captions for key steps and safety warnings.

**Testing.** The only real test is a novice attempting the task after one viewing. Each hesitation shows where the sequence, framing or narration needs revising.

caseStudies.title: Learning by watching

body.support:
In **2018**, a US research group called the **Pew Research Center** asked adults about YouTube.

About **half** of the people who used YouTube said it was **very important** for one thing. Working out how to do things they had never done before.

That is why so many workplaces now make short videos. They help new workers learn.

The survey was in the United States. But people in Australia watch how-to videos too.
body.core:
In **2018**, the **Pew Research Center**, a US research group, surveyed adults about how they use YouTube.

Of the people who used YouTube, **87%** said it was important for figuring out how to do things they hadn’t done before. **51%** said it was **very** important.

That’s why so many workplaces now use short videos to train staff and help customers. A good video can show what words alone can’t: where to put your hands, what the right result looks like, and what to avoid.

The survey was done in the United States, so it doesn’t tell us exactly about Australia. But how-to videos are a common way people learn here too.
body.extend:
In mid-**2018**, the **Pew Research Center** surveyed US adults about YouTube. Among YouTube users, **87%** said the site was important for figuring out how to do things they hadn’t done before, and **51%** said it was **very** important.

The finding helps explain why workplaces have embraced short instructional video for induction, safety and customer support. Video can show spatial and physical detail that is hard to describe in words: hand position, sequence, and what a correct result looks like.

There are limits. The survey covered the United States, so it doesn’t describe Australian habits directly. It measured what people said was important, not how well they learned. And popularity is not quality: many how-to videos are unclear, unsafe or wrong.

That makes design matter. A good workplace explainer is planned like a procedure, scripted like a talk, and tested on a real beginner.

source.name: Pew Research Center — “Many turn to YouTube for children’s content, news, how-to lessons” (November 2018)

model.text:
**[Wide shot: worker at a shop shelf]** “This is how to face up a shelf, so customers can find things fast. It takes about a minute.”
**[Close-up: hands pull a can forward]** “First, pull each product to the front edge.”
**[Close-up: label turned]** “Next, turn it so the label faces out.”
**[Caption: LIFT WITH YOUR LEGS]** “Before you lift a heavy box, bend your knees.”
**[Wide shot: neat shelf]** “Finally, step back and check. Every label faces out, every gap is filled. Done.”
why: Each line says what the camera shows, then what the narrator says.

teacher.overview: A VM 3&4 capstone. Students plan, storyboard, script and film an explainer video (under three minutes) teaching a task from a workplace they know, then test it on a novice and revise. It draws on procedural writing (Write the Procedure), structure and signposting (Plan Your Talk) and delivery (Nail the Delivery). The case study is a 2018 Pew Research Center survey: 51% of US YouTube users said the site is very important for figuring out how to do things they haven’t done before.
prep: Devices to film and edit (phones and a free editing app are enough).
A safe filming space; check risks for any trade or kitchen task.
Consent: students filming at a workplace need the employer’s permission; filming other people needs their consent.
Students should have done some On the Job and Speak Up courses first (this capstone requires two from each).

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 opening stating the task; 2 on-screen safety warning before the risk; 3 signposted first step with close-up; 4 exact detail (two seconds); 5 narration matches the picture; 6 finish check.

**Sort:** show — which button; how the clean nozzle looks. Say — why cleaning matters; when to do it. Both + caption — hot steam warning; 2-second purge.

**Case study:** in a 2018 US survey, 87% of YouTube users said it was important, and 51% very important, for learning how to do new things; video shows physical detail that words can’t; limits: US data, self-reported importance, and popularity isn’t quality.

realityCheck: **Safety and consent come first.** No dangerous tasks on camera; get workplace permission and consent from anyone filmed.
**Editing can eat time.** Set a strict limit, or allow a single continuous take with voice-over.
**Students without a job** can use a school task (canteen, library, workshop) or a home task with a work-like purpose.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Watching a novice follow the video is funny, humbling and very instructive.

levels.support: Aimed at about Years 3–4 reading: shorter article and case study, 6 key words, word bank and a three-shot storyboard.
levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with storyboard, signposted script, filming tips and testing.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: framing choices, word–image matching, captions, survey limits and novice testing.
